TITLE: Non-asymptotic sample complexity of KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We provide a non-asymptotic analysis of the sample complexity of KernelSHAP by showing that its strategy can be cast as an importance-weighted estimator, and then leverage uniform convergence results from importance-weighted averages to obtain a finite-sample error bound. Specifically, we show that with $m = O(d/\epsilon^2)$ samples, KernelSHAP's estimated Shapley values $\hat{\phi}$ satisfy $\mathbb{E} \|\hat{\phi} - \phi^* \|_2^2 \leq O(d^2 \epsilon^2 / m) + \epsilon^2$, where $\phi^*$ are the true Shapley values.
CONTROLS: First, we compare against the existing LeverageSHAP estimator, for which we already know a non-asymptotic error bound. To ensure our bound for KernelSHAP is not overly optimistic, we also analyze the worst-case scenario where samples are drawn with replacement, and compare against the baseline where the sample is drawn without replacement. Secondly, we investigate how the choice of sampling distribution (e.g., kernel weight or leverage scores) affects the error bound and computation time in practice.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: Our analysis will show that KernelSHAP's sample complexity and performance can be understood in terms of a tradeoff between bias, variance, and computational cost. We expect the derived bound to be useful in real-world applications where computational time is crucial; however, it could also fail for high-dimensional problems or extremely skewed data distributions.

TITLE: LeverageSHAP vs. KernelSHAP in Practical Settings
PROPOSAL: To better understand the practical performance of LeverageSHAP and KernelSHAP, we conduct an extensive empirical study on a range of high-dimensional datasets and models from different domains. We compare these two popular estimators in terms of their accuracy, robustness to overfitting, and computational efficiency, and also examine the effect of sampling rates and subset sizes on their performance.
CONTROLS: We consider both Shapley-value estimation and partial dependence plots as evaluation metrics, and for each experiment, we also report the results of the naive baseline (i.e., no regularization) and the EFIM estimator as a unweighted baseline. Furthermore, to highlight the robustness of our findings, we include a set of ablation studies to see how the choice of hyperparameters affects the performance of both LeverageSHAP and KernelSHAP.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: In real-world scenarios where overfitting is a concern, our study should provide nuanced insights into the relative performance of LeverageSHAP and KernelSHAP, and shed light on why one estimator is preferred over the other in different contexts. However, the bound may not be tight for very large-scale datasets.

TITLE: Efficient Estimation via Orthogonal Sequential Sampling
PROPOSAL: Motivated by the insights from our earlier work on LeverageSHAP vs. KernelSHAP, we explore an orthogonal sequential sampling strategy designed to improve the estimation efficiency of KernelSHAP. Our approach selects subsets sequentially, using information from previously selected subsets to inform the choice of the next subset to sample. By focusing on a dynamic subset of potentially informative features, our method adaptively identifies and prioritizes the most influential features in predicting the model's output.
CONTROLS: As an empirical evaluation, we compare our method against KernelSHAP's random sampling and leverage score-based approaches using several benchmark datasets. In addition, we include an analysis of the method's robustness to different sampling rates and problem complexities to demonstrate its adaptability.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: By engineered selection strategy, our sequentially samples method should consistently outperform random sampling, and this strategy allows the sampling mechanism to gradually identify high impact features reducing the burden on number of samples this is crucial when dealing with high dimensional dataset, however it's hard to quantify in this experimentation.

TITLE: Generalization of KernelSHAP to Infinite-Dimensional Feature Spaces
PROPOSAL: Given the widespread adoption of neural networks in real-world applications, we aim to extend the applicability of Shapley value estimation to infinite-dimensional feature spaces. By leveraging techniques from functional analysis and reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS), we develop a theoretical framework that generalizes KernelSHAP to the setting where the feature space is infinite-dimensional. Our approach involves representing the feature set as an element of the RKHS and estimating the Shapley values using a variational approach.
CONTROLS: To assess the efficacy of our extension, we evaluate it on several benchmark datasets where the feature space is approximately infinite-dimensional (e.g., natural images, text data). We also provide computational experiments to illustrate the practical benefits of our approach and compare it to competing methods.
COST: 672
PREDICTION: Our extension should be able to handle high-dimensional data where standard KernelSHAP or sequential sampling models are ineffective while might be useful when performing Data analysis for this particular data, however one might see a loss of interpretability when dealing with non-physical features.

TITLE: A Benchmarking Framework for Shapley Value Estimators
PROPOSAL: To provide a systematic and replicable evaluation of Shapley value estimators, we develop an open-source benchmarking framework that makes it easy to compare different methods in a fair and accurate manner. The framework includes a range of simulated and real-world datasets, evaluation metrics, and a user-friendly interface to configure and run experiments. By making our framework publicly available, we aim to facilitate the discovery of novel Shapley value estimators and provide a robust assessment of their performance.
CONTROLS: We benchmark our framework on several Shapley value estimators, including various kernel-based methods, LSH-based methods, and model-agnostic explanations. We also include a set of experiments to illustrate the robustness of our framework to varying problem complexities and data distributions.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: Our benchmarking framework should become a widely-used resource for the Shapley value estimation community, enabling the transparent comparison of different methods and accelerating research in this area. However, the framework's sensitivity to the choice of evaluation metric and problem complexity might necessitate careful consideration and tuning by users.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Enriching the Benchmarking Framework with Human Evaluation
PROPOSAL: While our benchmarking framework provides a quantitative evaluation of Shapley value estimators, human evaluation is essential to assess the practical relevance and interpretability of these explanations. We extend our framework to incorporate human evaluation, where a group of experts evaluates and annotate the explanations generated by different estimators. This enables us to quantify the agreement between human judgments and estimator outputs, providing insights into the reliability and usefulness of Shapley value explanations.
CONTROLS: We conduct a user study to elicit the annotation guidelines and perform a detailed analysis of the annotation process. We also investigate the impact of annotator expertise, explanation type, and problem complexity on the consistency of human judgments.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Our enriched framework should provide a more comprehensive understanding of Shapley value explanations, highlighting areas where estimators excel and where human judgment disagree. However, the subjectivity of human evaluation might introduce variability and require careful consideration of annotator biases and expertise.

TITLE: Understanding KernelSHAP's Failure Modes through Causal Analysis
PROPOSAL: Despite its popularity, KernelSHAP's performances can be sensitive to the specific problem and dataset, and it can fail to provide meaningful explanations under certain circumstances. We conduct a causal analysis to investigate the reasons behind KernelSHAP's failure modes, focusing on the impact of high-dimensional features, non-linear relationships, and endogeneity on its performance.
CONTROLS: We design a series of controlled experiments using both synthetic and real-world datasets to isolate the effects of these factors. We also compare the results of KernelSHAP with other Shapley value estimators to identify which ones are more robust to these challenges.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: Our causal analysis should provide valuable insights into the conditions under which KernelSHAP struggles, and identify areas for improvement to enhance its robustness and interpretability. However, the analysis might require complex causal modeling and techniques, which can be time-consuming and computationally expensive.

TITLE: Scalable Computation of Shapley Values using Parallel Processing
PROPOSAL: As the demand for Shapley value explanations grows, the need for efficient and scalable computation methods becomes increasingly important. We develop a parallel processing framework to compute Shapley values using multi-threading, multi-processing, and even distributed computing techniques. Our approach leverages the power of parallel computing to accelerate the computation of Shapley values for large datasets and models.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the performance of our framework using various parallelization strategies and explore the trade-offs between computation time, memory usage, and accuracy. We also compare our framework with existing serial computation methods to demonstrate its superiority.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: Our parallel processing framework should greatly accelerate the computation of Shapley values, enabling the widespread adoption of these explanations in high-stakes applications. However, the scalability of our framework might be limited by the availability of parallel computing resources and the difficulty of parallelizing certain operations.

TITLE: Formal Guarantees for the Robustness of Shapley Value Estimators
PROPOSAL: We develop a framework to provide formal guarantees on the robustness of Shapley value estimators against various types of perturbations, such as adversarial attacks, outliers, and noisy data. Our approach involves designing robust metrics to quantify the stability of Shapley value explanations and establishing bounds on the impact of perturbations on estimator performance.
CONTROLS: We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework using several robustness metrics and provide theoretical guarantees on the robustness of our estimators. We also compare our approach with existing methods that lack formal robustness guarantees.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Our framework should provide the first formal guarantees on the robustness of Shapley value estimators, enabling the development of more reliable and trustworthy explanations in high-stakes applications. However, the derivation of these guarantees might require sophisticated mathematical techniques and complex computations.

TITLE: Unifying KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP through a Common Framework
PROPOSAL: We provide a unifying framework that connects KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP, two popular Shapley value estimators, under a common theoretical umbrella. Our framework reveals the underlying connections between these two estimators and provides a deeper understanding of their strengths and weaknesses. We show that, in certain regimes, the two estimators are equivalent up to a simple transformation.
CONTROLS: We demonstrate the implications of our unifying framework using a range of experiments and provide insights into the behavior of both KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP under different conditions.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: Our unifying framework should provide a comprehensive understanding of the relationships between KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP, enabling the development of more effective and efficient Shapley value estimators. However, the complexity of our framework might make it challenging to interpret and apply in practice.

TITLE: Temporally Consistent Satellite Image Forecasting with Diffusion-Based Imitation Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop a diffusion-based image synthesis model that learns to imitate the temporal dynamics of a given sequence of satellite images. This is achieved by conditioning the diffusion model on the historical sequence and a sequence of temporal embeddings that capture the non-stationarity of the temporal process. The model learns to generate new images that maintain consistency with the observed temporal dynamics.
CONTROLS: Compare against a diffusion-based image synthesis model without temporal guidance, a model conditioned on text descriptions of the expected changes, and a physics-based model of satellite image formation.
COST: 7308.8
PREDICTION: This model will produce forecasts that are more temporally consistent and realistic than baseline models, but may struggle to capture rare or unusual events.

TITLE: Forecasting Evaluation with Temporal Consistency Metrics
PROPOSAL: Establish a set of metrics to assess the temporal consistency of satellite image forecasts. This includes metrics such as the Temporal Dependency Loss, which measures the extent to which the forecasted changes are consistent with the historical temporal dynamics, and the Temporal Fidelity Score, which evaluates the accuracy of the forecasted changes at each time step. These metrics will be compared to standard image quality metrics to assess their efficacy in evaluating temporally consistent forecasts.
CONTROLS: Compare against the mean squared error, peak signal-to-noise ratio, and other standard metrics.
COST: 1054.2
PREDICTION: This set of metrics will provide a more comprehensive evaluation of satellite image forecasts and will be found to be strongly correlated with user judgements of temporal consistency, but may still require fine-tuning for specific applications.

TITLE: Multimodal Fusion for Satellite Image Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Develop a multimodal fusion framework that integrates satellite image time series data with additional modalities, such as climate data, land use/land cover data, and socioeconomic data, to improve the accuracy and temporal consistency of satellite image forecasts. This will be achieved using a hierarchical fusion approach that combines features from each modality at different levels of abstraction.
CONTROLS: Compare against a model that only uses satellite image time series data, a model that incorporates a single additional modality, and a model that incorporates all additional modalities.

PREDICTION: This framework will improve the accuracy and temporal consistency of satellite image forecasts, but may require careful selection of the modalities and features to be used, and may be challenging to scale to large datasets.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE:  Investigating Adapter Parameters for Online Traffic Flow Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will extend the popular MoWoE (Multi-Output Wide & Ensemble) model used in traffic flow forecasting to incorporate an adapter module on the model's output. We will investigate, through ablation studies and hyperparameter tuning, which of the adapter's learnable parameters are most crucial for achieving accurate online predictions under distribution shift. Specifically, we will experiment with training several adapter configurations with different numbers of fully connected layers, activation functions, and learnable dimension reductions to assess how each factor affects the long-term performance of the model. 
CONTROLS: We will use time series splitting, with training on data up to week t-1 and evaluation on week t, and compare our results with an unadapted MoWoE model trained on the same datasets. We will also apply this technique to electricity consumption forecasting to assess transferability across domains. 
COST: 3
PREDICTION: We expect to identify key Adapter architectures that achieve robust, long-term forecasting performance with online training, but the models' sensitivity to overfitting may hinder their success during extreme distribution shifts.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE:  Analyzing Gradient Propagation in Deep Unfolding Architectures
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of gradient-based online learning methods in two typical deep unfolding architectures: a convolutional neural network (CNN) unfolded into an iterative algorithm using gradient-based optimization, and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) unfolded using the Deep Unfolded Network (DUN) framework. Our goal is to quantify how propagating information through unfolding layers affects convergence rates, dynamic regret, and accuracy under distribution shift, using real-world datasets from the experimental domains. 
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with online gradient descent (OGD) applied directly to the unfolded model parameters, and examine the influence of the depth and structure of unfolding layers on convergence and performance. 
COST: 5
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved convergence rates and accuracy for unfolding architectures under stationary distributions, but updates will accumulate more variance and become slower under distribution shift, potentially affecting long-term performance.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE:  Online Joint Optimization of Model and Statistics for Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to mitigating distribution shift by jointly optimizing model parameters and normalization statistics online. Using a grid-based spatial normalization scheme, we incorporate the computation of normalization statistics as an additional optimization objective that is updated online along with the model parameters. We will explore the effectiveness of this method using experiments on synthetic time series data as well as real-world datasets from traffic flow forecasting and electricity consumption forecasting, with a focus on both covariate shift and concept drift scenarios. 
CONTROLS: We will compare with a baseline method that updates only the normalization statistics online and another method that updates only the model parameters. Additionally, we will assess the impact of prior knowledge on the initial values of the normalization statistics versus optimal initial values learned during online training. 
COST: 8
PREDICTION: We anticipate this joint optimization method to effectively adapt the model to shifting data distributions by simultaneously updating the model's understanding of the underlying data trends and statistics, but we also anticipate challenges in maintaining accuracy during concept drift scenarios due to changes in underlying relationships.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE:  Investigating the Impact of Time-Aware Feedback Mechanisms on Multi-Step Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will explore the effects of delayed and noisy feedback on multi-step forecasting accuracy and propose novel time-aware feedback mechanisms that account for the temporal dependencies in time series data. Our primary goal is to investigate whether incorporating time-aware information into the feedback loop can mitigate the adverse effects of delayed and noisy feedback, leading to improved online forecasting performance. We will experiment with different architectures that explicitly model the effect of time on feedback, including models that incorporate temporal convolutional layers and attention mechanisms that focus on past feedback. 
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed methods with several baseline approaches that ignore or naively account for time-aware feedback, including online ridge regression, where adjustments are made at each step solely based on the available partial results of previous forecasts. 
COST: 6.85
PREDICTION: We expect to see improvements in multi-step forecasting accuracy when time-aware feedback mechanisms are incorporated, particularly under conditions with significant delayed and noisy feedback, but potential difficulties may arise with the increased model complexity and computational costs.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE:  Investigating the Impact of Time-Aware Feedback Mechanisms on Multi-Step Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to specifically focus on combining time-aware feedback mechanisms with deep unfolding architectures, with the aim of developing a dual-layered learning framework that leverages the strengths of both techniques. By explicitly modeling temporal dependencies in the feedback loop and propagating information through unfolding layers, we anticipate this combined approach to yield improved accuracy and robustness for multi-step forecasting tasks under conditions with delayed and noisy feedback. 
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our combined framework with each individual component and evaluate its effectiveness against several alternative approaches that either ignore time-aware feedback or naively incorporate unfolding structures. We will also investigate the impact of different unfolding layer configurations on the performance of the combined framework. 
COST: 7
PREDICTION: We expect our revised approach to demonstrate enhanced forecasting capabilities under challenging conditions, but may encounter increased computational costs and the need for careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance the performance of both the time-aware feedback mechanism and the unfolding architecture.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE:  Regularized Online Model Distillation for Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We introduce a regularized online model distillation framework for adapting pre-trained models to evolving time series distributions. By incorporating a distillation objective that seeks to minimize the difference between the pre-trained model's predictions and those of an updated teacher model, we aim to bypass the need for explicitly identifying and updating sensitive model parameters online. We will investigate the effectiveness of our approach using experiments on synthetic and real-world time series data from various domains, including traffic flow forecasting and electricity consumption forecasting. 
CONTROLS: We will compare our method with state-of-the-art online adaptation techniques and evaluate the impact of different regularization strategies on the performance of the distillation framework. 
COST: 10
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our regularized online model distillation framework will provide a more straightforward and efficient approach to adapting pre-trained models to evolving time series distributions, although challenges may arise in balancing the competing objectives of model adaptation and regularization.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE:  Online Joint Optimization of Model and Statistics for Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We refine our previous proposal to incorporate a kernel-based learning approach for adaptively learning the covariance structure of the data in a time-dependent manner. By integrating a kernel-based change-point detection method into our online joint optimization framework, we aim to more effectively capture changes in the underlying distribution of the time series data, leading to improved forecasting performance under concept drift scenarios. 
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised approach with both the original online joint optimization method and alternative kernel-based learning approaches that ignore the temporal dependencies in the data, and assess the impact of different kernel choices and hyperparameters on the performance of the revised framework. 
COST: 8.7
PREDICTION: We expect our revised online joint optimization method to demonstrate enhanced robustness and adaptability under concept drift scenarios, although the increased computational cost and the need for careful tuning of hyperparameters may challenge its practical implementation.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE:  Robust Online Transfer Learning for Time Series Forecasting under Distribution Shift
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel robust online transfer learning framework for adapting pre-trained models to new, unknown distributions that may exhibit significant differences from the original training data. By incorporating a variational uncertainty estimate of the model's predictions into the transfer learning objective, we aim to enhance the robustness and adaptability of the model under distribution shift scenarios. We will investigate the effectiveness of our approach using experiments on real-world time series data from various domains, including traffic flow forecasting and weather forecasting. 
CONTROLS: We will compare our method with state-of-the-art online transfer learning techniques and evaluate the impact of different uncertainty estimation strategies on the performance of the transfer learning framework. 
COST: 12
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our robust online transfer learning framework will provide a more effective approach to adapting pre-trained models to new, unknown distributions, although challenges may arise in balancing the competing objectives of transfer learning and uncertainty estimation.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE:  Adaptive Buffering for Online Time Series Forecasting under Concept Drift
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive buffering approach for online time series forecasting that dynamically adjusts the size and composition of the buffer based on the observed concept drift and other factors. By incorporating an exploration-exploitation strategy to balance the trade-off between exploration and exploitation of new samples, we aim to improve the adaptability and robustness of the model under concept drift scenarios. We will investigate the effectiveness of our approach using experiments on real-world time series data from various domains. 
CONTROLS: We will compare our method with state-of-the-art buffering techniques and evaluate the impact of different exploration-exploitation strategies on the performance of the adaptive buffering framework. 
COST: 15
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our adaptive buffering approach will provide a more effective way to adapt to concept drift scenarios by dynamically adjusting the buffer size and composition, although challenges may arise in balancing the competing objectives of exploration and exploitation.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE:  A Unified Framework for Online Time Series Forecasting under Distribution Shift
PROPOSAL: We propose a unified framework for online time series forecasting that integrates multiple techniques, including adapter parameters, joint optimization of model and statistics, regularized online model distillation, robust online transfer learning, and adaptive buffering, to adapt to distribution shift scenarios. Our goal is to develop a general-purpose framework that can be easily extended to accommodate new techniques and domain-specific knowledge. We will investigate the effectiveness of our unified framework using experiments on real-world time series data from various domains. 
CONTROLS: We will compare our framework with state-of-the-art online time series forecasting techniques and evaluate the impact of individual components on the overall performance of the framework.
COST: 21
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our unified framework will provide a more comprehensive and adaptable approach to online time series forecasting under distribution shift scenarios, although challenges may arise in balancing the trade-off between different components and ensuring seamless integration.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Hybrid Retrieval with Multimodal Late Interaction
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the performance of the ColPali-based encoder with and without a lightweight dense text retriever, using hybrid retrieval to aggregate their outputs at query time. The baseline consists of the ColPali-based encoder alone, while the control explores adding the dense text retriever to the ColPali-based encoder. We predict that the combination of the two will improve the trade-off between retrieval quality, online latency, and index memory compared with scaling up the representations of the ColPali-based encoder alone.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: ColPali-based encoder alone; (2) Control: ColPali-based encoder + dense text retriever (no hybrid retrieval); (3) Strong negative control: Empty ranking (random order of documents).
COST: 3600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the hybrid approach to outperform the ColPali-based encoder alone, with a significant improvement in online latency and index memory usage while maintaining or slightly improving retrieval quality. However, this performance gain might come at the cost of minor losses in top-1 accuracy compared to using the dense text retriever alone.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Designing Multimodal Representation Fusion Schemes
PROPOSAL: This work investigates various methods for fusing the representations of the ColPali-based encoder and the dense text retriever in the hybrid retrieval framework. Specifically, we examine (1) concatenation, (2) element-wise summation, (3) late interaction, (4) multimodal attention, and (5) a neural network-based fusion method. Our goal is to identify the most effective fusion strategy that complements the signals of both retrievers. We predict that the neural network-based fusion method and multimodal attention will perform competitively.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Concatenation; (2) State-of-the-art multimodal late interaction (control); (3) Empty fusion (no fusion, compare with baseline hybrid retrieval).
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the best-performing fusion method to improve upon the baseline hybrid retrieval approach by 5-10% in retrieval quality, with some methods likely underperforming due to added complexity or increased latency.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Query and Document Reworking
PROPOSAL: This experiment explores whether reworking query and document representations to match the modalities of the other retriever can improve the performance of the hybrid approach. Specifically, we will (1) apply text-to-image and image-to-text transformers to the query representations of the dense text retriever and the ColPali-based encoder, respectively, and (2) rework document representations in a similar fashion. Our aim is to determine whether adapting representations to the modalities of both retrievers can enhance the hybrid system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: No reworking; (2) Control: Reworking a single modality (e.g., rework query representations of the dense text retriever); (3) Hybrid retrieval without reworking (control).
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that reworking query and document representations can improve the hybrid approach by 2-5% in retrieval quality, although the gains might be marginal and depend on the specific application.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Evaluating Heterogeneity-Aware Aggregation Methods
PROPOSAL: In the hybrid approach, the signals from the two retrievers must be combined despite differing dimensionalities and scales. This proposal evaluates various heterogeneity-aware aggregation methods, such as (1) dimensionality reduction-based methods (e.g., PCA, t-SNE), (2) scale-aware normalization techniques, and (3) heterogeneity-invariant metrics (e.g., set similarity, distributional similarity). Our goal is to identify methods that effectively handle the heterogeneity while preserving the rich interactions within the representation spaces.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Simple average or concatenation; (2) Control: No heterogeneity-aware aggregation (naive aggregation); (3) State-of-the-art dimensionality reduction method (control).
COST: 1350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that heterogeneity-aware aggregation methods will improve the hybrid approach by 5-10% in retrieval quality, particularly for multimodal representations with large dimensionalities and scales. However, the choice of method will depend on the specifics of the representations and application.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Composing Multiple Weak Models for Robust Hybrid Retrieval
PROPOSAL: Rather than depending on a single lightweight retriever, this proposal investigates composing multiple weak models, each capturing a different aspect of the data, to robustify the hybrid approach. Specifically, we will (1) train and combine multiple instances of the dense text retriever, each with a different architecture or hyperparameter set, and (2) explore combining the outputs of these models using majority voting or an ensemble learning method. Our aim is to assess whether combining multiple weak models can improve the robustness and reliability of the hybrid system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Single lightweight retriever; (2) Control: No composition (single instance of the retriever); (3) Combining multiple instances of a robust model (control).
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that composing multiple weak models can improve the robustness and reliability of the hybrid approach, particularly in scenarios with noisy or ambiguous queries and documents. However, the gains might come at the cost of increased latency and computational resources.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Hybrid Retrieval with Multimodal Late Interaction
